Yes and no. The card faces will be very similar, differing only in layout
and errata (which will of course mostly be good, although we may have a
few misrules like Rotschreck cast into stone, or at least ink). The backs
will differ, and so anybody playing a mixed deck will be playing with a
marked deck, permitting a wide variety of cheating techniques,
particularly for "degenerate" decks (here meaning decks with only a few
types of cards).

Another idea for dealing with the change in card backs -

your predator can cut your library or crypt immediately
before you draw from it, any time you are entitled
to draw from it.

Slows things down a little, but if anything it turns
the card-back markings into a liability. The info about
the card type is only available after you've already
decided to draw, so it doesn't let you see the future;
and if you have followed some kind of marking scheme,
if your opponents figure it out, it gives them info
about what you just drew.

A difference in attitude, I suppose. Although I'm not terribly happy
about the change, it's done. There's nothing I can do about that.
So my reaction is to look for ways to make the best of it; and for
that purpose, I don't give a fig whose fault it is. This
leads to the following strategies for me :

(1) I won't purposely build marked decks; in fact I'll go
out of my way to "un-mark" them by including cards with both
back designs for cards I use multiples of.

(2) I'll play with people who trust me not to abuse the card
backs, and I'll play with people whom I trust not to abuse the
card backs. If we occasionally get minor bits of intelligence
because we know our card mix very well, so it goes. If no one
is abusing it, no one's gaining much more of an advantage...

suggest things like frequent deck-cutting or draws from the bottom
of the deck to appease my suspicious opponents. Although I
don't like drawing from the bottom of the deck, seems to cause
more problems than it fixes.

eliminate the card marking advantage. Just as long as it's done
occasionally and unpredictably. Myself, if I were playing with a group
who didn't trust each other enough for 1 and 2 above to pacify them,
I'd rather have a little deck gymnastics and slow-down of the game
than to never play with expansion cards.

: I think it is a bad idea and we wouldn't even need

: to discuss this if WotC had some sense.

Again, a difference in attitude. Now that it's done, I don't
care about placing blame - I just want to find ways to
continue playing and enjoy the evolution of the game with the
new cards. And, from my end, this isn't meant to be disrespectful
though it probably sounds it (btw, I wasn't offended at all by the tone
of your post, James)...but if your reaction to the situation will
be to play with your old cards and cry in your beer about how
WotC made it impossible for you to use the expansions...well...
I bet I know which of us is going to have more fun with the game.

Friends:

Hi, this is Mavra, aka Peter, the janitor at Wizards of the Coast. Several of
you have written me with your concerns on the name change of our game Jyhad to
V:TES, and the subsequent removal of the word Jyhad from the contents of the
game. This letter is a response to those letters, and the letters I haven't
yet received.

This was a tough decision as you can probably imagine. And in truth, I think
it was one of those times we as a company genuinely faced a no-win scenario.

Making the change seriously risks killing the game and pissing off our
customer base. We have never suffered from the delusion that this would
somehow help the sales or popularity of the game.

Keeping it the way it is, I believe, is immoral. It's as simple as that. I
can't have a game like this in my catalog and look our Middle East distributors
straight in the eye.

I know a lot of you don't feel that there's anything immoral about using the
word Jyhad in a game. But our products are reaching new customers and
countries that never cared about traditional roleplaying games and such, and
may of them disagree. Of course I didn't see this as a problem originally,
but I have a middle-class WASP background and spent many years thinking the
United States was the center of the universe and that the thoughts of people
in the Middle East didn't really matter. Fortunately I met Beverly and she
taught me how much of an ass hole I was for thinking that way, and so at the
age of twenty-eight I grew up and got a life.

Folks, we just can't pull this kind of crap anymore. We're a big company now,
selling games all over the world, way outside the niche markets we started in.
We have a duty to represent ourselves as a mature company that is sensitive
to the political, religious, gender, and ethnic issues that are facing society
today. This change is in response to that duty.

We could lose millions of dollars over this decision.

I don't care. We have to do what we think is right.

Mavra!
(Peter D. Adkison, Janitor, Wizards of the Coast, Inc.)

rotates his half of cards when he cuts, make a mental note that somewhere
in the middle of the deck, the pattern will change. Granted, it's not as
easy as vampire/jyhad named backs, but it is a pretty effective way of
marking cards, and works well. Works especially well if all your friends
are lazy and insist that you must shuffle all the cards and get the
murder/weapon/room cards into the confidential file in Clue. Needless to

The short answer is that the name change, and the card back change happened
for two reasons: moral reasons, and marketing reasons. The reason any
particular person may have heard early in this decision-making process
would have depended on which aspect the person they were asking was
focusing on. When the potential change first came up, the people I talked
to were focusing more on changing the game name for marketing reasons.
The moral reasons (which I still think had more impact on changing the card
backs than on changing the name in the first place) weren't explained, at
least not to me, until later.

Both reasons for changing the name and card backs existed all along, but
individuals tended to focus more on one reason or another at first. This is
part of the reason for the earlier confusion as to whether any, or all, of
the card backs would be changing; those who were focusing more on the
marketing aspects leaned in favor of not changing the card backs at all,
but further discussions with people with other concerns resulted in all
of the card backs being changed.

>and the opinions expressed around here.

This is basically a long argument that I am misusing the term "politically
correct" and is thus fairly irrelevant to the point I'm trying to make.
Perhaps I am misusing it, perhaps not. To me, "politically correct" has always
connoted the desire to enforce linguistic censorship based on sensitivity to
members of other social/ethnic/racial/sexual/whatever groups, although it also
occasionally arises in describing other liberal causes. Anyway, this is what
I'm talking about when I use the term. To clarify (so we don't get
sidetracked) I'm not trying to paint WotC as a organization espousing radical
views. Sometimes even "political correctness" as I'm using the term is quite
justified. In fact, the phenomenon would never have arisen were there not a
need for a certain amount of it. I just feel that its not justified for WotC
to self-censor itself in this case, particularly in view of the damage that
that self-censorship is causing the people who purchased your product.

>>The reason that "Jyhad" was not identified as "offensive" by those who
>>thought to inscribe it on the backs of your trading cards was because they
>>could not conceive of any strong reason it should be. And the reason it
>>came as such a surprise to WotC to discover some folks might consider it
>>offensive was that those "some folks" were simply wrong in this case...

>I find it extremely strange that you would try to figure out for someone
>else whether that person is offended by something or not. Having an
>opinion as to whether they *ought* to be offended is one thing, but whether
>they actually are?

(Heh. We're going to have agree to disagree after we argue about it a
_little_ bit, huh? :) :) :) )

You are quite correct that we can't tell anyone how to feel. If they feel
offended, they'll feel offended regardless of whether we think they "ought"
to or not. But that's not the question, here. Whether they "ought" to feel
offended is very much the real question. A mugger may very sincerely feel
offended if I don't give him all my ready cash but frankly, that doesn't
constitute a moral argument that I should give it to him.

The same principle applies to WotC using the word "Jyhad". People may feel
offended by it, but is this a reason in and of itself for WotC to change their
card backs? No, not by itself. Were they justified in feeling that way, one
could suggest that that's enough of a reason to take this action, although I
also have a further argument that even so, it would weigh poorly against the
real damage being done to your customers by the card back change. In short,
the ends don't justify the means.

This is precisely the logic that I've been attempting to address. What you're
saying, in essence, is that you don't wish to make a value judgement about
the question of whether "Jyhad" should be offensive to some population group.
Yet the question of changing the card backs clearly involves weighing the
damage the being done to your first wave Jyhad customers vs. the interests
of that population group. When you decline to make that value judgement and
simply accept the claims (that "Jyhad" is offensive), you are not being at all
fair to the opposing interests.

You MUST make that value judgement to be fair and it's clear that you didn't.
At the same time, the statements and actions of WotC in the course of
justifying the card back change made it clear to us that you made a value
judgement about changing card backs that most players feel underrates its
significance. Is it any wonder you're encountered a great deal of resentment

Why do you feel you have to try? If the card back decision is part of the

where it simply isn't going to sell. Was it necessary to experiment with

>what is and isn't acceptable content for our products. Freedom of speech
>does not include a carte blanche right to run roughshod over a peoples'

Actually, while I agree that at the end of the day, WotC has the right to make
whatever decision on this matter that they would, I would pick one nit: There
is absolutely nothing whatsoever about the concept of Freedom of Speech that
involves limiting ones own speech based on the beliefs and sensibilities of
others. Quite the opposite - Freedom of Speech is distinctly _OPPOSED_ to
the concept that what others think matters when it comes time for me to decide
what I think it's necessary to say. If you don't understand that, Tom, you
don't understand what's important about this great principle.

come to the considered judgement that "jihad" is offensive, you should be quite
willing and even eager to present this to your customers.

Fred

>words people consider dirty, but you do not, is going to lead to
>totoletarian rule I guess.

Others may see it this way but I'd like to make it clear that I do not.
This is more the rationale of those who bitched about the "demon sweep"
in Magic's 4th Edition of "The Gathering". I guess I thought that was
kind of silly, myself, since the demon sweep didn't actually hurt anything.

Political correctness basically says, "We don't want to make a value judgement
when someone else says they're offended by something. We just accept on
blind faith that they're being harmed by the offensive 'thing' (whatever it
happens to be) since we don't have their cultural frame of reference to say
whether they're correct or not." I don't agree with this logic. Making no
decision _IS_ making a decision. In this case, it accords the assertion (that
something is truly offensive and despicable, etc.) the highest possible
validity, when it may not really deserve that.

That's a harmless enough when there are no tradeoffs involved. For instance,
when black people want to be called "Black" and not "Negro" or when Native
Americans prefer that moniker to "Indian", that's fine - it's no particular
problem for people to comply with their wishes. But when you have to weigh
their desires against some other real world material consideration, that's
a different thing. When that happens, you must make the value judgement - even
from your imperfect frame of reference - or you're not being fair.

Fred

We were very aware of the impact the change would have on the existing
customer base, and gave that due to consideration during the process.
Just because the decision didn't come down as the existing customer base
would have liked, doesn't mean that the customer base was ignored.

>You MUST make that value judgement to be fair and it's clear that you didn't.

We did make a value judgment. Our judgment disagrees with yours. That's
no reason to blow ours off, or to claim that we didn't make one at all.

Because focusing on the existing customer base is the best way to stagnate
a game. If we just cater to that customer base, and never make any allowances
for potential customers who have problems with the game, then the game
will stagnate as the existing customers move on to other things despite
our best efforts.

culture, and pasttimes. That includes pushing the entire line of products,
not just one or two projects here and there. No, we don't really expect
V:TES to ever be any bigger than, say, horror movies, but it's clear that
it could be a lot bigger than what the hobby industry is capable of supporting.

>Was it necessary to experiment with
>Jyhad, as opposed to developing other CCGs that are would be much more likely
>to appeal to larger markets?

What other CCGs? Magic is already tearing into the mainstream with no effort
on our part. V:TES is the only other deckmaster game we have. The longer
we wait to try to push another CCG, the harder it will be.

>Actually, while I agree that at the end of the day, WotC has the right to make

economic policies that a people must live by (or try to change), and a *game*

you or whatever.

Case one: The name of the game was a mistake, which I argued
from the moment I first heard of it, before the game
was even release, and I was virtually alone in my
opinion. Anyone else who had an opinion was already
a Masquerade fan (I had virtually no idea what it

made and they made it.

good friend of my ultimately refused to play the game
precisely because of the name, believing that it was
potentially a conflict of religious beliefs, and might
be perceived as insulting by people who hold those
beliefs. And then WotC had to make a decision, and they
made one. The timing was bad, and in reality, they were
and are painted into a corner, and no bandaid is going
to instantly make the damage caused by their initial
short-sighted error go away. It's gonna hurt no matter
what they do, but they decided, rightly, that the name
Jyhad was a mistake, and that it would be better to
excise it completely, now, take the pain, and to
hopefully come out better on the other side. But it
was their hard decision and they made it.

Case last: So the last suggestion is made that the way to make
it all right is:

: ... a _responsible_ action by WotC: A trade-in...

Have any of you even thought about, let alone
calculated, the potential expense of such a trade-in?
I have seen this suggestion bandied about as if
it were more than reasonble, and my same innate sense
that told me that Jyhad was a bad name tells me that
such a suggestion, at this point, is nuts. The ailment
in no way whatsoever justifies this cure, and the
cure is potentially more destructive than a simple
preemptive amputation. A suggestion to just drop
the game completely makes more sense, economically,
than to reprint and resupply all of the cards
printed so far. The ignorance of basic economics,
statistics, and just plain business sense displayed
by people here, and the selfish egocentric gimme-opinions
that proliferate on this and similir subjects indicate
to me that the primordial limbic functions are way
too uninhibited and the higher cortical functions are
way too suppressed, apparently caused by a combination
testosterone/silicon overload.

Case Ultimate: Do any of you care about anything else in your
lives as passionately as you do about these games?

A Trade In? You tell us how much it will cost and
otherwise justify why it makes good business sense,
beyond the foaming rantings of your own tribal unit,
and I will gladly withdraw and retract my rant.

rob

general reputation as a company) as well. Whether the cost would be worth
the gain depends on the cost (which few posters really know anything about)
and the (undoubtably highly speculative) estimates about the gain.

Fred

James R. McClure Jr. (jmcc...@e-mail.kdp-baptist.louisville.edu) wrote:

: ro...@cray.com (Robert M Derrick) wrote:
: >Someone wrote:
: >: ... a _responsible_ action by WotC: A trade-in...

: Peace Rob,

Mir, Shanti, Salaam, Hey Wa, James.

I won't belabour your entire response, suffice it to say that we
view self-control and offense at differing points along the
grey continuum of behaviour.

: ... I even asked how many cards and what percentage of the whole

: print run had been exchanged during the two previous card exchanges (Legends
: and Antiquities).

And those numbers are?

: ... I have checked on what percentage of Antiquities and Legends cards

: were exchanged and expect that a similar percentage of Jyhad cards would be
: exchanged.

I do not know what kind of exchange was made in Antiquities, so I cannot
comment on that (and I'd be glad to be enlightened). But I do know about
Legends, and it is clear that there is no reasonable comparison, even
without knowing all of the numbered details. Even if more Legends cards
were printed than Jyhad, there is still no comparison. The Legends'
exchange was only for uncommons, and at the most WotC only had to
expect that at worst half of the uncommons printed would need to
be exchanged, and that the cards sent in for exchange would in turn
be used to provide the other half of the exchange. And, there was
no identical card exchange, but the returned cards were likely to
be randomly chosen from the opposite set (tho' due to the small
numbers involved, I understand that WotC did attempt to fill some
wish lists)

On the other hand, a Jyhad exchange, at worst, consists of the
entire print run of Jyhad from day one, and includes many peoples
2000+ cards collections, and while folks like me might not be as
broken up about the "back change" as you, many of us would still
be tempted to send ours in for replacement anyway -- nifty new cards
with nifty new formats -- and the potential impact on WotC is likely
even more than just a total wash on the entire Jyhad cost/profit
to date, but the expense of reproducing the entire print run of
Jyhad, and then sorting, by hand, millions of cards
to provide everyone with the identical set they had before...

: [unless, of course, WotC is wrong about how few of the current

: players are angered by the changing of the card backs]

So the real question comes down to, how many Jyhad players, that is, of
the entire customer base of Jyhad since day one, are "angered by the changing
of the card backs", plus those that, while not angry, would take advantage
of a card exchange anyway?

Above you indicate that you think this number is rather low, based on
past numbers from Antiquities and Legends.

You also hint above and elsewhere that you think this number is large,
speaking of the "customer base", and how much damage this will cause to
the game, since so many are angered.

So, which is it? Of the 100% of all Jyhad buyers since day one, what
percentage are angered by the change? If it's large, then a card
exchange is not feasable, plus, that large percentage of the customer
base is wiped out, and so WotC takes it in the pants either way.
It's a no-win situation.

Or, that number is small, or at least not significant enough to matter,
economically, and WotC believes, with some justification, that there
is also a whole new world of potential customers out there that will
ultimately dwarf the current vocal curmudgeons and Rikinites. Life
does go on, New Coke is a notable exception, of course, but since the
analogy is poor enough already, let's not bring it up again.

Now, you claim to have the numbers, so let's see them.
My entire diatribe was to ask someone to justify what I considered
to be an extraordinarily foolish suggestion. I challenged anyone
to support it with data rather than invective. And other than your
McCarthyesque content-free rhetoric, the response was thundering
silence.

How many Antiquities cards were printed, what were the terms of the
exchange, and how many cards were exchanged? Did new cards have to
be printed to replace the old, and at what cost? What were the labor
costs involved? Who paid the postage, to and fro?

How many Legends uncommon cards were printed, and how many cards were
exchanged? What were the labor costs involved? Who paid the postage, to
and fro?

How many Jyhad cards were printed, and what terms of exchange are
you proposing? What is the expected case scenario, and what is the
worst case scenario? How many new cards will have to be printed
for the exchange alone? What will the labor costs be, and who will
pay the postage, to and fro?

: The question for WotC is, "Which costs more: a card exchange or losing a segment

: of our customers (and all the customers they would have created)?" It seems
: like a simple question (and answer) to me.

Me too, and I think the answer is not the one you think it is, and I
think that WotC has come to the same painful conclusion. I have met
my fair share of "alpha/beta magic" players who are insensed over
[insert latest WotC move here] and who are never going to play again,
and their impact on the game has been about the same as Arthur Dent's
impact on the bulldozer.

Of course, your numbers, James, could show me wrong...

rob

I wasn't given specific numbers, just approximate percentages. I didn't save the
emails; I have only my memory to go on. I was told that in the case of both AQ &
LE the exchange percentage was very low (<2%).

far more likely to be returned an others far more likely to be requested, so I'm
not sure how successful they were at filling wish lists.

>On the other hand, a Jyhad exchange, at worst, consists of the

Given past card return/exchange rates, I'd say that the probability of a worst case
scenario (or even a near-worst case) is zero. I'm sure the parts of WotC opposed to
a card exchange would use this as a scare tactic to disuade the other parts of WotC
from doing the right thing.

>: [unless, of course, WotC is wrong about how few of the current
>: players are angered by the changing of the card backs]
>

>the entire customer base of Jyhad since day one, are "angered by the changing
>of the card backs", plus those that, while not angry, would take advantage
>of a card exchange anyway?

Not exactly. It comes down to how many people would spend the time and effort to
ship all their cards (regardless of reasoning). Given the attitudes of most
Americans, even the annoyed ones will be unlikely to expend the effort to get all
their cards replaced.

>Above you indicate that you think this number is rather low, based on
>past numbers from Antiquities and Legends.

I'm working on a hypothesis based on the percentages that WotC provided me, which
were quite low.

>You also hint above and elsewhere that you think this number is large,
>speaking of the "customer base", and how much damage this will cause to
>the game, since so many are angered.

I've stated that it appears to me, from talking to players local to me and from
reading this newsgroup, that a large percentage of the established Jyhad customer
base is angered by the decision by WotC to change the card backs. I've never said
that a large number would exchange cards.

>So, which is it? Of the 100% of all Jyhad buyers since day one, what
>percentage are angered by the change? If it's large, then a card
>exchange is not feasable, plus, that large percentage of the customer
>base is wiped out, and so WotC takes it in the pants either way.
>It's a no-win situation.

Again, you are misconstruing what I said. I said most (>50%) of the established
customer base was angry with the change. I said that past card trade-ins have been
very small percentages of the print run. These are not contradictory statements.

If a no-win scenario now exists for WotC (and I don't know if one does or not), then
they have "painted themselves into a corner." The consumers didn't force WotC to
publish a teriffic game, poorly market it, and then make further poor decisions on
how to "save" that game.

>Or, that number is small, or at least not significant enough to matter,
>economically, and WotC believes, with some justification, that there
>is also a whole new world of potential customers out there that will
>ultimately dwarf the current vocal curmudgeons and Rikinites. Life
>does go on, New Coke is a notable exception, of course, but since the
>analogy is poor enough already, let's not bring it up again.

These are your opinions. The idea that there is some vast, untapped customer pool
out there is fanciful. Gamers as a whole are a small segment of the population.
Complex strategy games, like Jyhad, are only interesting to a segment of the gamer
population. Expecting to find an El-dorado of customers just by changing the games
name is silly.

>Now, you claim to have the numbers, so let's see them.
>My entire diatribe was to ask someone to justify what I considered
>to be an extraordinarily foolish suggestion. I challenged anyone
>to support it with data rather than invective. And other than your
>McCarthyesque content-free rhetoric, the response was thundering
>silence.

Nope, I don't have the actual numbers, just percentages. I don't consider a card
exchange to be "foolish" and neither do most of the people that have responded to
my initial suggestion for one. There are apparently enough "fools" working for WotC
that they have seriously entertained the notion of doing a card exchange.

Now, as far as my posts being "McCarthyesque [no relation] content-free rhetoric",
well it seems that you and Tom Wylie agree on that. Fortunately, everyone else on
this newsgroup seems to feel that I post useful and informative data. If I've
misrepresented myself, I welcome corrections from other net.citizens.

One more thing. Most posters will see a reply [like mine] to a challenge/question
[like yours] and seeing that the reply is correct and that they mostly agree with it,
they will chose not to waste time and bandwidth "me too"ing. That is what you are
seeing, Rob. Again, if I'm making a mistake here, I welcome correction.

>How many Antiquities cards were printed, what were the terms of the
>exchange, and how many cards were exchanged? Did new cards have to
>be printed to replace the old, and at what cost? What were the labor
>costs involved? Who paid the postage, to and fro?

I don't know. Send it cards, get cards back. I don't know. I don't know. I don't
know. The consumer (to) and WotC (fro).

>How many Legends uncommon cards were printed, and how many cards were
>exchanged? What were the labor costs involved? Who paid the postage, to
>and fro?

See above.

>How many Jyhad cards were printed, and what terms of exchange are
>you proposing? What is the expected case scenario, and what is the
>worst case scenario? How many new cards will have to be printed
>for the exchange alone? What will the labor costs be, and who will
>pay the postage, to and fro?

I believe the number bandied about is 130 million. Equal exchange is what I suggest.
It is the only truely fair way. I expect a similar percentage of exchange to
previous exchange (~2%). I don't have access to enough data to formulate a valid
"worst case scenario". None as cards from the normal print run will do. I don't know
what WotCs labor costs are. Consumer (to) and WotC (fro).

>: The question for WotC is, "Which costs more: a card exchange or losing a segment
>: of our customers (and all the customers they would have created)?" It seems
>: like a simple question (and answer) to me.
>
>Me too, and I think the answer is not the one you think it is, and I
>think that WotC has come to the same painful conclusion. I have met
>my fair share of "alpha/beta magic" players who are insensed over
>[insert latest WotC move here] and who are never going to play again,
>and their impact on the game has been about the same as Arthur Dent's
>impact on the bulldozer.

Thanks for agreeing with me. Arthur Dent held the bulldozer effectively motionless
until Ford convinced him to go to the pub. I guess we'll have to agree to disagree
on which is the bigger loss: the old customers (and all their progeny) or a card
exchange. We can't disagree on which one is the conscientious thing for WotC to do.
A company that claims to care about their customers (and potential customers) as
much as WotC does only has one choice when it comes to fixing a mistake that that
company has made (such as this one is).
